To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) children's implicit and explicit attitudes are not always consistent, (2) the development of children's attitudes is sensitive to the cultural context in which they are raised, and (3) the development of attitudes towards religious outgroups in India may differ from attitudes towards racial groups in the United States.
implicit ingroup preferences are found for both caste and religion in India, with religion playing a more protective role than caste.
implicit attitudes towards caste in India parallel those towards race in the US, and that implicit attitudes towards religion in India are the opposite of those towards race in US.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how social categorization operates in a culture that differs markedly from that in which the vast majority of social categorization research is conducted.
the role of religion as a social category, the development of implicit attitudes towards religious groups, and the role of religion in insulating ingroup evaluations.
the development of inter-group attitudes and how these attitudes vary as a function of social context.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the results of this research suggest that the development of implicit social attitudes in India is similar to that found in Western countries, but that the results also indicate that religion may play an important role in insulating individuals from the negative effects of stigma.
the development of inter-group attitudes depends on the nature of the intergroup context and that the development of implicit attitudes is more complex than previously believed.
religion is more important than caste in determining implicit intergroup attitudes in children.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
implicit evaluations of outgroups are not universal and that religion may be a powerful source of identity for children.
implicit attitudes are not a universal feature of social categorization, and that they are not necessarily predictive of explicit attitudes.
implicit attitudes towards social groups may be more complex than previously thought, with different social categories playing different roles in different cultures.
The main takeaway from our work is that

implicit attitudes are not necessarily the same as explicit attitudes, and that implicit and explicit attitudes may be differentially sensitive to the social categories of different cultural contexts.

social categories are not interchangeable: different categories have different implications for the development of attitudes and that the development of attitudes is not uniform across all social categories.
social categories that are salient in different cultures have different effects on the development of children's implicit attitudes.
